Each cycle must be completed before leaving its attachment vertex, and each has two possible directions. Thus there are 2·2=4 routes. audits.mathematicalReason: One valid solution uses impartial-game values. Set g(0)=0. Removing r consecutive bricks, where r is 1 or 2, from a wall of length n leaves wall lengths i and n-r-i. Thus g(n) is the mex of the values g(i) XOR g(n-r-i) over all legal r and i. This gives g(1),...,g(6)=1,2,3,1,4,3. The five starting positions consequently have xor values 3,0,3,1,2, respectively. Only (6,2,1) is a losing position for the player to move, so Beth can guarantee a win there. This solves the task but does not supply a defensible catalog mapping for adversarial game-state classification. The candidate's unresolved scope assessment is preserved.

audits.mathematicalReason: Every semicircle has radius 1. The six interior crossings of adjacent semicircles form a regular hexagon of side 1. Along each side of this inner hexagon, the shaded region excludes a circular segment with radius 1 and central angle 60 degrees. Each segment has area π/6−√3/4. Therefore the shaded area is 3√3/2−6(π/6−√3/4)=3√3−π. The alternative overlap calculation also works: the outer hexagon has area 6√3, the six semicircles have total area 3π, and each of the six adjacent-pair lenses has area π/3−√3/2. Nonadjacent semicircles do not overlap, and there are no triple overlaps, giving 6√3−3π+6(π/3−√3/2)=3√3−π. Both are valid geometric area methods, but the finite-set counting node should not be assigned to the latter.
